summary: Works that arrive from OpenAlex with no abstract must have one fetched from PubMed by DOI BEFORE the relevance and PICO gates run, because a work gated on its title alone is gated on a property of OpenAlex's coverage rather than of its own content. The step is bounded (a per-run DOI cap and its own deadline), spends that budget on the works the gates currently EXCLUDE, and reports what it recovered, what stayed unresolved and what the cap skipped, so a reader can tell how much of the analysis still rests on titles.
reason: 18% of works have no abstract at the source (52 of 295 archived studies; 51 of those 52 carry a DOI), and the abstract-less path is not neutral: such a work only has to clear one distinct claim stem instead of two, so it enters the corpus on weaker evidence than everything around it. Three findings must survive a regen or this comes back wrong. (1) BACKFILL BEFORE THE GATES, NOT AFTER — supplying an abstract is exactly what changes their verdicts, and it cuts both ways, since a backfilled work's relevance bar rises from one stem to two and it can therefore be pushed OUT. (2) ONE esearch PER DOI, never an OR-batched query: measured against the live API on the 51 abstract-less archived works, per-DOI lookups resolve 41 while OR-ing 20 `<doi>[doi]` terms into one query resolves 20, so the cheap form silently loses half the yield. (3) PATH-SCOPE THE efetch XML — a PubmedArticle carries ArticleId and AbstractText elements that belong to its REFERENCES and to OtherAbstract translations, and a parser reading them from anywhere in the subtree bound 8 of 41 records to a cited paper's DOI, which would attach an unrelated abstract to a real work; reading only PubmedData/ArticleIdList/ArticleId and MedlineCitation/Article/Abstract/AbstractText makes that unrepresentable. The cap exists because one lookup costs ~631ms at PubMed's keyless pace and a maximum-size fetch produced up to 51 candidates, so an uncapped step would add ~30s to a query; whatever number a regen picks, it must be measured against both the candidate count at the maximum --limit and that per-lookup cost, and the operator escape hatch (SC_NO_ABSTRACT_BACKFILL) must remain.
validated_outcome: go build clean; go test green across the module except the pre-existing TestPICOGateIsDeadForBenefitClaims failure, which reproduces identically on a clean HEAD (verified by stashing this work) and belongs to the earlier PICO benefit-claim extension. Benefit and risk were measured in one live run over three claims at the command's default --limit 40 (120 works, 70 kept, 50 excluded): 15 of 15 backfillable gate-excluded works resolved and 10 re-entered the corpus, while 0 of the 4 backfillable survivors were pushed out — net +10 works, 8.3% of the corpus, with no measured loss. Cap sizing measured separately at --limit 200: 124 of 600 fetched works (20.7%) were abstract-less with a DOI, per claim 42/31/51, of which 79% were gate-excluded; one DOI lookup costs ~631ms keyless, putting a cap of 50 at ~32s worst case, which is why the step's deadline is 45s. Both measurements are reproducible rather than logged: internal/cli/zz_live_backfill_probe_test.go re-runs them under SC_PROBE_LIVE=1 and is skipped otherwise, and the full analysis is written up as Part 4 of internal/scengine/testdata/MISSING_ABSTRACT_ANALYSIS.md. The risk side rests on 4 observations and is recorded as such, not as proof that no work can ever be lost. NOT established: whether the 10 recovered works are on-topic evidence rather than passing mentions — they cleared both shipped gates, which for PICO means their abstract names the intervention and the outcome, but no human adjudicated them.
